newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Pope's message to Bosnia briefly takes centre stage.
newsitem.headline: Pope's message to Bosnia briefly takes centre stage.

text.p: Pope John Paul II's visit to Sarajevo over the weekend made history for the Catholic church in Bosnia and his appeals for reconciliation drowned out -- at least temporarily -- the customary din of nationalist rhetoric.
It was the first time a Pope had set foot in Sarajevo, a city where the Catholic faith has had to co-exist with other religions for centuries.
The Bosnian capital welcomed him as a long lost friend and tried to put on its best face despite damage caused by more than three years of war.

The Pope's calls for tolerance were greeted warmly by leaders of other religions, but diplomats say it will take more than goodwill from the Vatican to reverse the religious intolerance which fuelled the Bosnian war.
Western envoys said the visit was welcome but were uncertain whether anything had changed as a result.
"He even talked yesterday about forgiveness which is a very strong word and powerful word to use in the circumstances here," said Carl Bildt, the international High Represenative to Bosnia.
"I hope this will have an impact. I really wish of course that this would have been able to reach out somewhat more to the mountains over there (in Serb territory)."
The first test will be whether the Pope's own church can practise what he preached at an open-air mass on Sunday: "Offer forgiveness and receive peace."
Religious leaders in former Yugoslavia rarely speak of forgiveness, usually stressing how their own people have suffered at the hands of others.
The Catholic church in Bosnia includes clergy, such as Cardinal Vinko Puljic, who fervently support restoring religious co-existence.

But there are priests outside Sarajevo, especially in the southwestern Herzegovina region, who strike a much harder line. Franciscan friars in Herzegovina see Islam as a mortal threat and advocate a strict separation of religious communities.
The Pope's speeches, which celebrated cultural diversity and tolerance, provided a sharp contrast to the nationalist rhetoric offered up by Bosnia Croat media.
By travelling to Sarajevo, now a predominantly Moslem city, the Pope sent a symbolic message to Croat nationalists that co-existence was possible.
By meeting Islamic leaders and clergy from the Serbian Orthodox church, he may have helped to breathe life into efforts to open a dialogue between the three major faiths.
During the war, the Serbian church openly sided with nationalists who pursued "ethnic cleansing" campaigns, expelling Moslems and Croats from their homes and blowing up ancient mosques.
The Orthodox clergy, like the Serb political leadership, has yet to show any sign that it is ready to help those who were expelled to recover their homes.
In the weeks before the papal visit, Moslem politicians launched a public discussion questioning whether it was time to reject the multi-ethnic ideal and build a state for Bosnian Moslems.
Diplomats say it is too early to declare Bosnia dead, but they say the country may be doomed if Serb, Croat and Moslem nationalist parties remain in power.
Without a change in the political leadership and democratic reforms, local religious figures will continue to be used as tools for nationalist goals, they say.
